**Step 1 — Scene:** A small meal of roasted chicken, baby carrots, and a whole Asian pear.

**Step 2 — Vessel:** A dinner plate, approximately **26 cm** in diameter. Area = 3.14 × 13² ≈ **531 cm²**.

**Steps 3–7 — Items, area, volume, weight, and energy:**

The heights below are average heights across each food’s footprint, rather than maximum heights.

| Visible item | Plate area covered | Area × average height = volume | Bulk density | Estimated weight | kcal/100 g | Energy |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Whole Asian pear | 16% | 85 cm² × 4 cm = 340 ml | 0.90 g/ml | 306 g | 42 | 129 kcal |
| Roasted chicken, skin-on | 11% | 58 cm² × 1.8 cm = 104 ml | 0.95 g/ml | 99 g | 230 | 228 kcal |
| Four baby carrots | 6% | 32 cm² × 1.5 cm = 48 ml | 0.85 g/ml | 41 g | 41 | 17 kcal |
| Visible cooking-fat sheen | 2% | 11 cm² × 0.2 cm ≈ 2.2 ml | 0.90 g/ml | 2 g | 880 | 18 kcal |

The projected food coverage totals approximately **35%** of the plate. Compact, whole fruit and carrots use higher densities than loosely piled cut produce. Chicken weight represents the edible portion; the exposed bone is excluded.

**Step 8 — Sanity check:** Approximately **448 g and 392 kcal** is plausible: the large pear contributes most of the weight, while the chicken contributes most of the energy. The main uncertainties are the pear’s size and the amount of edible chicken.
